investigate:shielding.summary:
SHIELDING LENS. Neither experiments/local_fields.md nor experiments/fields_study.md existed when I checked, so nothing here was cross-checked against them. All numbers are from the scratch script listed under files; nothing in the repo was modified.

**Plain answers.** Can a local field shield like Earth's? No, by 6 to 20 orders of magnitude for the array, and by 1 to 3 orders even for the best laboratory magnets against cosmic rays. Can an RF field block radiation or other radio waves? No. The useful versions are receive-side nulling, passive shielding, and observing space weather.

**1. How Earth shields, and why scale decides.** The Lorentz force bends a charge on a gyroradius rho = p/(qB), so what matters is rigidity R = pc/q, or equivalently B*rho = R/c. A shield of size L needs B*L of roughly B*rho. Light and radio carry no charge and pass straight through.

| Particle | Rigidity | B*L needed |
|---|---|---|
| Solar-wind proton, 1 keV | 1.4 MV | 0.0046 T·m |
| Solar energetic proton, 100 MeV | 0.44 GV | 1.5 T·m |
| Galactic cosmic-ray proton, 1 GeV | 1.7 GV | 5.7 T·m |
| Galactic cosmic-ray proton, 10 GeV | 10.9 GV | 36 T·m |
| Ground-level muon, 4 GeV mean | 4.1 GV | 14 T·m |

| Field source | B*L available |
|---|---|
| Earth, equatorial integral from surface outward (B0·RE/2) | about 96 T·m |
| LHC dipole (8.33 T x 14.3 m, 50 mm bore) | 119 T·m |
| Spacecraft superconducting toroid studies (8.6-16.8 m diameter) | 5.4-11.4 T·m |
| 3 T MRI over 1 m | 3 T·m |
| NdFeB block | 0.025 T·m |
| The array, even if its field were static (5 nT peak at 1 m) | about 5e-9 T·m |

- **Earth:** the Stormer vertical cutoff is B0·RE·c/4, about 14.9 GV·cos^4(latitude): 14 GV at the equator, 0.9 GV at 60 degrees.
- **Solar wind:** it is stopped collectively where B^2/(2·mu0) equals ram pressure, which needs only 58 nT, but over more than the 70-100 km ion scale. That reproduces the roughly 10 RE magnetopause. Lunar crustal anomalies (500 nT at most, hundreds of km) do form mini-magnetospheres.
- **Spacecraft studies:** the toroids stop solar particle events and only partly stop galactic cosmic rays.
- **Ground level:** the 10.3 m water-equivalent atmosphere does most of the work. Muons arrive from all directions and would need 14 T·m.

**2. RF as a particle shield.** An oscillating field gives zero net first-order deflection. The residual is the ponderomotive energy Up = e^2·E^2/(4·m·omega^2). At 1 m from the 433 MHz whips (38.9 mW EIRP, 1.08 V/m rms):
- Electrons get 1.4e-8 eV, against a thermal 0.026 eV.
- Protons get 7.5e-12 eV, which is 1e14 short of a solar-wind proton and 1e20 short of a 1 GeV cosmic ray.
- Reaching 1 keV for protons would need 1.8e7 V/m, six times air breakdown.

**3. Shielding radio.** Maxwell's equations are linear in vacuum, so waves superpose and pass through each other.
- **Active cancellation:** it makes a 10 dB quiet pocket about lambda/10 across: 6.9 cm at 433 MHz, 1.9 cm at GPS L1, 1.2 cm at 2.44 GHz, 0.5 cm at 5.8 GHz. It only works for signals you hold a coherent copy of, and the energy is redistributed into brighter fringes elsewhere.
- **Receive nulling:** this is the array's real shield. Four coherent channels give 3 nulls. A 1 degree / 0.1 dB calibration error gives about 34 dB depth; the 0.15 degree calibration target gives about 50 dB (estimates). Commercial 7-element GNSS antennas quote 20-40 dB.
- **Passive:** Faraday cages work because copper's skin depth is 2 um at 1 GHz; mu-metal diverts static and low-frequency magnetic flux.

**4. What local fields produce.**
- **Exposure:** the FCC general-population limit is f/1500 mW/cm^2 from 300-1500 MHz and 1.0 mW/cm^2 above. The array reaches it only within about 3.3 cm (433 MHz) or 0.7 cm (2.44 GHz).
- **Heating:** an oven is about 1 kW; the array's 39 mW fully absorbed would warm 1 g of water by 0.009 K/s at most.
- **Plasma:** air breaks down near 3 MV/m (1.2 MW/cm^2 plane-wave equivalent). The array's 3.6 V/m at 0.3 m is 1e6 short in field and 1e12 in power.
- **Wireless power:** 118 uW at 1 m and 13 uW at 3 m (433 MHz, 0 dBi receiver), which is tag-trickle level.

**5. Watching Earth's shield instead.**
- **Sun:** the quiet Sun (70-200 sfu) raises panel noise by 0.3-0.9 %, detectable only by beam-switching or drift scans. A 1e4 sfu burst gives about +1.5 dB and a 1e6 sfu burst (December 2006) about +16 dB. The F10.7 index frequency, 2.8 GHz, is in the panel band.
- **Ionosphere:** with bladeRF A on L1 and B on L2, 1 TECU is 0.105 m (0.35 ns) of differential delay; storms move tens of TECU. The S4 amplitude index comes from 50 Hz signal-to-noise; multi-antenna multipath rejection is a real array advantage.

findings.claim: Shielding is the Lorentz force bending charged particles; the governing quantity is rigidity R=pc/q with B*rho=R/c. Stormer vertical cutoff for a dipole is about 14.9 GV*cos^4(lat)/r^2 (r in Earth radii); my derivation B0*RE*c/4 with B0=30 uT gives 14.3 GV at the equator, 8.1 GV at 30 deg, 3.6 GV at 45 deg, 0.9 GV at 60 deg. Photons and radio waves are uncharged and unaffected.
findings.source: https://www.spenvis.oma.be/ecss/e_st_10_04c/ecss_13_08_00.htm ; derivation in calc.py

findings.claim: B*rho (the B*L needed for about 1 rad of bending): solar-wind proton 1 keV = 0.0046 T·m (1.4 MV); SEP proton 10 MeV = 0.46 T·m; SEP 100 MeV = 1.48 T·m (0.44 GV); GCR proton 1 GeV = 5.7 T·m (1.7 GV); GCR 10 GeV = 36 T·m (10.9 GV); sea-level muon at 4 GeV mean energy = 13.7 T·m (4.1 GV). Gyroradius in a 50 uT field: 91 m, 9 km, 30 km, 113 km, 727 km, 274 km respectively.
findings.source: derivation (relativistic pc=sqrt(T^2+2Tmc^2)) in calc.py; muon mean energy about 4 GeV and vertical intensity about 70 m^-2 s^-1 sr^-1 from the PDG cosmic-ray review https://ccwww.kek.jp/pdg/2006/reviews/cosmicrayrpp.pdf

findings.claim: Earth: B0*RE = 191 T·m; equatorial integral of the dipole field from the surface outward = B0*RE/2 = about 96 T·m. Laboratory: NdFeB block 0.5 T x 5 cm = 0.025 T·m; 3 T MRI x 1 m = 3 T·m; 10 T solenoid x 0.2 m = 2 T·m; one LHC dipole 8.33 T x 14.3 m = 119 T·m but only inside a 50 mm bore at 1.9 K. Reaching Earth-class B*L around a room-sized volume takes accelerator-class superconducting magnets.
findings.source: derivation in calc.py; LHC dipole parameters https://jinst.sissa.it/LHC/LHCmachine/ch03.pdf ; magnet sizes other than LHC are illustrative estimates

findings.claim: Superconducting-toroid studies reach 5.4, 8.3 and 11.4 T·m for outer diameters of 8.6, 12.3 and 16.8 m (EU SR2S, MgB2, at most 4 T at the conductor); the NASA NIAC study used 8 m coils at 1 T for 8 T·m. An 8 T·m toroid could eliminate solar-particle-event risk but gives only partial protection against galactic cosmic rays, consistent with the 1.5 T·m (100 MeV) versus 5.7-36 T·m (1-10 GeV) requirements.
findings.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4896949 ; https://iris.unitn.it/retrieve/e3835196-29c7-72ef-e053-3705fe0ad821/vuolo2016.pdf ; https://indico.cern.ch/event/445667/contributions/2562900/attachments/1514058/2363200/MT-25_2ORAC06.pdf

findings.topic: Solar wind is the easy case, but needs size
findings.claim: Solar wind (estimate: 5 protons/cm^3 at 400 km/s) has ram pressure 1.3 nPa, balanced by a field of only 58 nT; with the dipole field doubled at the boundary this puts the magnetopause at 10.1 RE. The deflection is collective and requires a structure larger than the proton gyroradius (70 km in 60 nT) or ion inertial length (102 km). Lunar crustal anomalies (500 nT at most, hundreds of km) form mini-magnetospheres, with a collisionless-shock electric field doing the deflecting; laboratory plasma-wind-tunnel experiments reproduce this at scaled size. A bench-top field in air has no plasma flow to stand off, and the solar wind never reaches the ground anyway.
findings.source: derivation in calc.py (solar-wind density and speed are typical values, unsourced estimate); Bamford et al. https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/1207.2076 ; https://www.ralspace.stfc.ac.uk/Pages/Natural-Mini-magnetospheres-on-the-Moon.aspx

findings.topic: What actually protects people at ground level
findings.claim: The atmosphere is 101325 Pa / g = 10,330 kg/m^2, i.e. 10.3 m water-equivalent of mass shielding; NASA describes the magnetosphere and atmosphere together as the protection. Ground-level muons are secondaries made in the atmosphere, arrive from all directions and need about 14 T·m; neutral secondaries (neutrons, gammas) ignore magnetic fields. No practical local magnetic shield exists for them; mass (rock, water, lead) is the working answer.
findings.source: derivation; https://climate.nasa.gov/news/3105/ ; https://ccwww.kek.jp/pdg/2006/reviews/cosmicrayrpp.pdf

findings.claim: From REDESIGN.md full-drive EIRP: four whips at 433 MHz, +15.9 dBm (38.9 mW): 3.1 mW/m^2, 1.08 V/m rms, 5.1 nT peak at 1 m (3.6 V/m, 17 nT at 0.3 m). Panel at 2.44 GHz, +8.1 dBm (6.5 mW): 0.44 V/m rms, 2.1 nT peak at 1 m. At the 15.249 level (-1.25 dBm): 0.15 V/m, 0.7 nT at 1 m. The RF magnetic field is about 1e-4 of Earth's 50 uT surface field and it alternates, so even treated as static its B*L of about 5e-9 T·m is 1e6 below the solar-wind requirement and over 1e9 below a 1 GeV cosmic ray.
findings.source: /Users/ascalva/Documents/code/sdr_array/array16/REDESIGN.md section 7 (line 109) plus far-field derivation S=EIRP/(4 pi r^2), E=sqrt(S*377) in calc.py

findings.claim: An oscillating field gives no net first-order deflection; the cycle-averaged effect is the ponderomotive potential Up=e^2 E^2/(4 m omega^2). At 1 m from the 433 MHz whips: Up(electron)=1.4e-8 eV (quiver amplitude 36 nm), Up(proton)=7.5e-12 eV. Compare thermal 0.026 eV, solar-wind proton 1e3 eV (1e14 short), 100 MeV SEP (1e19 short), 1 GeV GCR (1e20 short). At 2.44 GHz from the panel: Up(e)=7e-11 eV. Up(proton)=1 keV at 433 MHz would need 1.8e7 V/m peak (4e11 W/m^2), about 6x the air-breakdown field, so the air would ionise first. Answer: no.
findings.source: derivation in calc.py; formula https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponderomotive_energy (URL not fetched this session)

findings.topic: A field cannot block a radio wave
findings.claim: Maxwell's equations in vacuum/air are linear, so fields superpose and waves pass through each other unchanged; no field of any shape (knotted or not) blocks another. What is possible is destructive interference at chosen points using a coherent copy of the unwanted signal. The energy is not destroyed: the interference term redistributes it into brighter fringes elsewhere, or, if the canceller is within about a wavelength of the source or receiver, it loads the source or absorbs the power itself.
findings.source: derivation (superposition; total power = sum of the two powers plus an interference term that integrates to zero for well-separated sources)

findings.claim: For a remote cancelling source in a diffuse (multipath) field the 10 dB quiet zone is a sphere about lambda/10 across, a theoretical limit established for acoustics that carries over to any scalar wave field. For the array: 6.9 cm at 433 MHz, 3.3 cm at 915 MHz, 1.9 cm at 1575 MHz, 1.2 cm at 2.44 GHz, 0.5 cm at 5.8 GHz. It needs amplitude and phase matched to about 10 % for 20 dB and 1 % for 40 dB, and works only for signals the array can copy coherently. The array can only cancel fields no stronger than its own (0.15-1 V/m at 1 m).
findings.source: https://www.ioa.org.uk/system/files/publications/SJ%20ELLIOTT%20P%20JOSEPH%20PA%20NELSON%20ACTIVE%20CONTROL%20IN%20DIFFUSE%20SOUND%20FIELDS.pdf ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.04191 ; wavelengths in calc.py; transfer from acoustics to RF is my inference

findings.claim: An N-channel array places N-1 independent nulls: 3 with the four coherent bladeRF channels (e.g. four whips at GPS L1 as a small anti-jam antenna). Null depth is about -20*log10(rms complex weight error): 1 deg and 0.1 dB gives about 34 dB; the 0.15 deg calibration target in REDESIGN.md would allow about 50 dB (estimates). Commercial 7-element GNSS anti-jam antennas quote 6 nulls at 20-40 dB typical; one measured prototype got only 5-7 dB against a simulated 40 dB because of combiner errors and mutual coupling, so calibration is the limit. Nothing is transmitted, so no exposure or licensing issue.
findings.source: https://www.l3harris.com/sites/default/files/2020-10/antenna-n202-series-sas.pdf ; https://www.gnss.ca/brochures/gajt-710ml-ps.html ; https://hexagondownloads.blob.core.windows.net/public/Novatel/assets/Documents/Papers/ion_2001/ion_2001.pdf ; depth formula is my estimate

findings.claim: Conductive enclosures (Faraday cages) work at RF because induced currents cancel the field: copper skin depth is 2.1 um at 1 GHz but 9.2 mm at 50 Hz, so they fail for slow magnetic fields. Static and low-frequency magnetic fields are shielded by high-permeability mu-metal, which shunts flux around the volume; reported shielding factors are 1e3-1e5 for one or two layers. This is the practical way to make a 'local magnetosphere' for an instrument: it removes Earth's field from a box, but it does not stop particles.
findings.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mu-metal ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.01519.pdf ; skin depth derived in calc.py (rho_Cu=1.68e-8 ohm·m)

findings.claim: FCC general-population maximum permissible exposure (47 CFR 1.1310 Table 1): f/1500 mW/cm^2 for 300-1500 MHz (0.29 at 433 MHz, 0.61 at 915 MHz) and 1.0 mW/cm^2 (10 W/m^2, 61 V/m rms) for 1.5-100 GHz, 30-minute average. By the far-field formula the array reaches these only within about 3.3 cm (433 MHz, +15.9 dBm) or 0.7 cm (2.44 GHz, +8.1 dBm); at 1 m it is 1e3-1e4 below the limit. Microwave ovens may leak up to 5 mW/cm^2 at 5 cm in service (21 CFR 1030.10).
findings.source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-1/subpart-I/section-1.1310 ; https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/1030.10 ; distances from calc.py (near-field values are rough estimates)

findings.topic: What local fields can produce: heating, plasma, power
findings.claim: Heating: a 1 kW oven spread over a 0.09 m^2 cavity cross-section is about 11 kW/m^2, roughly 2 kV/m rms plane-wave-equivalent (estimate); the array's total 39 mW, if fully absorbed in 1 g of water, warms it 0.009 K/s at most. Plasma: air breaks down near 3 MV/m (DC/low-frequency figure; the microwave threshold depends on frequency, pressure and pulse length), equivalent to 1.2 MW/cm^2; the array's 3.6 V/m at 0.3 m is 1e6 short in field and 1e12 in power. Wireless power (Friis, 0 dBi receiver): 433 MHz gives 118 uW at 1 m, 13 uW at 3 m, 1.2 uW at 10 m; 915 MHz gives 20 uW at 1 m; 2.44 GHz gives 0.6 uW at 1 m. That is enough to trickle-power a harvesting tag at 1-3 m (rectifier threshold around -20 dBm is my estimate); a 4 W EIRP RFID reader gives 27 uW at 10 m.
findings.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dielectric_strength ; derivations in calc.py; RFID 4 W EIRP (1 W + 6 dBi under 15.247) https://rfid4u.com/rfid-regulations/

findings.claim: 1 sfu = 1e-22 W/m^2/Hz; the F10.7 index is measured at 2800 MHz, inside the panel band, with a solar-minimum floor near 65 sfu. With the panel G/T of -20.2 to -12.5 dB/K from REDESIGN.md, dT/Tsys = S*(G/T)*lambda^2/(8 pi k): quiet Sun 70-200 sfu gives 0.3-0.9 % (0.013-0.04 dB), 13-46 sigma of ideal radiometer noise in 1 s at 20 MHz but below ordinary gain drift, so it needs beam-switching on/off the Sun or a drift scan. A 1e4 sfu burst gives +42 % (about 1.5 dB); 1e6 sfu gives about 16 dB. A single whip at L-band (2 dBi, Tsys 200 K assumed) sees +3 dB for 1e4 sfu and +20 dB for 1e6 sfu.
findings.source: https://www.spaceweather.gov/phenomena/f107-cm-radio-emissions ; https://www.stce.be/news/374/welcome.html ; /Users/ascalva/Documents/code/sdr_array/array16/REDESIGN.md line 90 ; derivation in calc.py

findings.claim: The 6 December 2006 solar radio burst exceeded 1,000,000 sfu at L-band, about 10x any earlier recorded event, and made many GPS receivers on the sunlit side lose track; dual-frequency civilian receivers were worst hit. This is a natural broadband jammer the array could record directly as a noise-floor rise on every channel at once (coming from the Sun's direction, which the array can confirm by direction finding).
findings.source: Cerruti et al. 2008, https://doi.org/10.1029/2007SW000375 ; https://digitalcommons.njit.edu/fac_pubs/12574 ; https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2007/04/070407145619.htm

findings.claim: Ionospheric group delay is 40.3*TEC/f^2: 1 TECU (1e16 e/m^2) = 0.162 m at L1, 0.267 m at L2, 2.1 m at 433 MHz. The L1-L2 differential is 0.105 m (0.35 ns) per TECU, i.e. 2.85 TECU per ns, so storm-time changes of tens of TECU are metres of differential delay. L1 (1575.42) and L2 (1227.60) are 348 MHz apart, wider than one AD9361's bandwidth, so use bladeRF A on L1 and B on L2 (shared 10 MHz reference) with the whips. S4 is the normalised standard deviation of signal intensity; about 0.6 is moderate and 0.9 strong at L1. Phase-slip probability on L2 is about 10x that on L1 in G3 storms.
findings.source: https://gps.ece.cornell.edu/SpaceWeatherIntro_ed2_10-31-06_ed.pdf ; https://angeo.copernicus.org/articles/27/2101/2009/angeo-27-2101-2009.pdf ; https://angeo.copernicus.org/articles/24/1581/2006/angeo-24-1581-2006.pdf ; derivation in calc.py; receiver plan from REDESIGN.md lines 57, 78

findings.topic: Knot as a 'stable field over a volume' (shielding view)
findings.claim: An RF knot or vortex pattern from the array is a steady interference pattern only while the transmitters run; at milliwatt levels it exerts no confining or deflecting force (ponderomotive energy about 1e-8 eV) and stores negligible energy. The real 'field geometry holding something over a volume' is static twisted magnetic field lines in plasma confinement (tokamak and stellarator rotational transform), where field strength times size sets what is held, exactly as in the B*L table.
findings.source: derivation above; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational_transform (URL not fetched this session)

open_questions: experiments/local_fields.md and experiments/fields_study.md did not exist when I checked, so overlap with the parallel studies (especially the Sun and vortex sections) is unverified.
Solar-wind density and speed (5 per cm^3, 400 km/s) and the sea-level dose contribution of muons are typical textbook values I did not source this session.

The lambda/10 quiet-zone limit is an acoustics result; I applied it to RF by analogy (scalar diffuse field). A short simulation with the array's own geometry would confirm the size for a vector EM field and a 4- or 16-element canceller.
Microwave-frequency air-breakdown threshold was not sourced; the 3 MV/m figure is the DC/low-frequency value. Low-pressure plasma ignition thresholds were not researched.
Transmitting a cancelling copy of someone else's signal may count as interference under FCC rules even at Part 15 levels; this was not checked. Receive-side nulling avoids the question.
Whether the 10 MHz TCXO is quiet enough for phase-scintillation (sigma-phi) measurement is untested; amplitude S4 and dual-frequency TEC should not depend on it.
Null-depth figures for the array (34-50 dB) are estimates from calibration-error arithmetic, not measurements; mutual coupling between whips will likely set the real limit.
How often solar bursts exceed 1e3-1e4 sfu at 1-6 GHz (the rate of detectable events for this array) was not sourced.

investigate:structured.summary:
Lens: uses of knotted and structured field geometries. Neither /Users/ascalva/Documents/code/sdr_array/array16/experiments/local_fields.md nor fields_study.md existed when I looked, so nothing here was checked against them. Numbers are my derivations (script and results in the scratch folder) unless a URL is given; several older citations are DOIs from memory, not fetched, and are marked medium.

**1. Is a knot a "stable field over a volume"? Half yes, mostly no.**
- Yes, topologically. A vortex line is a curve of exact zero amplitude that the phase winds around. Small perturbations move the curve but cannot untie it; that requires two lines to cross and reconnect, the same class of event as magnetic reconnection.
- The protection is finite. Optical knots survived weak turbulence but reconnected under stronger turbulence (Pires 2025); knotted water vortices untie themselves within about 0.5 s (Kleckner and Irvine).
- No, energetically. The knot is made of darkness, not of held energy. At the 15.245 limit (18.75 dBm EIRP) the field 0.3 m away is 5 V/m rms, 0.066 W/m². A 0.3 m cube holds about 6 pJ, replaced every 1 ns. Stop driving and it is gone in nanoseconds.
- The self-sustaining version exists only in plasma. Magnetic helicity (linkage of field lines) is nearly conserved in a conductor, so a plasma relaxes to a twisted minimum-energy state (Taylor); spheromaks, reversed-field pinches and the tokamak's twisted field rest on this. It needs currents in a conducting medium, which free-space radio lacks.

**2. What structured fields are used for elsewhere.** Optical tweezers and spanners (trapping, torque from orbital angular momentum), STED microscopy (doughnut null beats the diffraction limit), rotational Doppler (spin measurement), dark-core atom traps, information encoding in orbital angular momentum, framed knots and skyrmions, and plasma confinement.

**3. Radio versions at this project's scale.**
- Forces and torques: no.
  - Total force on a perfect absorber is P/c: 16 pN for 4.7 mW radiated (estimate: 12 dB array gain). Pressure at 0.3 m is 2.2e-10 Pa, about 1e5 below the 20 µPa threshold of hearing.
  - Gradient force on a 1 mm water drop is 4e-17 N against 4e-5 N of weight (ratio 1e-12).
  - Torque is l·P/ω = 3.1e-13 N·m per unit l at 2.45 GHz and 1.3e-13 at 5.8 GHz. A frictionless 1 g, 5 cm foil disc would need about 2 hours for its first turn. The published microwave torque experiment measured about 1e-8 N·m, roughly 3e4 times more.
  - Why optics manages it: P/c is the same at any wavelength, but an object matched to the wavelength scales in mass as λ³, about 1e15 heavier at 12 cm than at 1 µm. Even the FCC exposure limit (1 mW/cm²) gives only 3.3e-8 Pa.
- Shielding like Earth's field: no. A 1 GeV proton has rigidity 5.66 T·m; Earth manages with 30 µT because the gyroradius (190 km) is small against a field tens of thousands of km deep. One metre needs about 6 T static. The array's field is 1.7e-8 T, alternating at GHz, with ponderomotive energy about 1e-8 eV.
- Rotational Doppler: yes, the best demo.
  - Shift is Δf = l·Ω/2π, independent of carrier, so it is identical at 2.4 and 5.8 GHz: 1200 rpm gives 20 Hz per unit l (60 Hz at l=3); 3000 rpm gives 50 Hz per l.
  - No vortex transmit is needed: illuminate plainly on-axis, receive on a ring, and decompose digitally into modes. Mode l shows a line at l·Ω/2π whose sign gives the rotation sense, which one on-axis antenna cannot see.
  - The carrier sets how many modes are resolvable (estimate, 15 cm rotor at 0.5 m): 112 mm ring about 2 at 2.44 GHz and 4 at 5.8; 225 mm ring about 3 and 7.
  - Echo is about -40 dBm (2.45 GHz) and -48 dBm (5.8 GHz) at 1 m for 0.01 m², so leakage and clutter limit it, not noise.
- Nulls as precision tools: yes. The radio counterpart of the STED doughnut is the monopulse or null-steering null: a 25° beam locates to about 0.1° at 40 dB SNR.
- Vortex modes for capacity: no gain; they are a subset of MIMO and fade fast with distance.
- Knots as information: weak; reading one needs a 3-D field scan.
- Polarisation-structure probing: blocked, since the panel is single-polarisation and the whips vertical.

**Ranking (reality × demo value):** 1 rotational Doppler on a fan or drill; 2 null steering and quiet zones; 3 near-field focal-spot targeting; 4 mapping a knotted null with a probe; 5 vortex multiplexing; 6 torque; 7 trapping and shielding.

findings.claim: Knotted and linked vortex lines (curves of zero amplitude) have been built in laser beams, including isolated trefoil and other knots designed with a numerical optimiser. They are structurally stable: perturbations deform the curve, and topology changes only when lines cross and reconnect.
findings.source: https://www.nature.com/articles/nphys1504 ; https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/29392 (Leach et al., Nature 432, 165, 2004)

findings.claim: Optical knots keep their invariant in weak turbulence but lose it through reconnections in stronger turbulence; a follow-up preprint reports persistence falling below 26 % in moderate turbulence and to 4-8 % in the strongest case tested. Knotted water vortices untie through reconnections within about 0.5 s.
findings.source: https://ideas.repec.org/a/nat/natcom/v16y2025i1d10.1038_s41467-025-57827-1.html ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.08836 ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/1310.3321 ; https://www.nature.com/articles/nphys2560.pdf

findings.claim: A driven radio knot stores almost nothing. At 18.75 dBm EIRP and 0.3 m: S = 0.066 W/m² (6.6 µW/cm²), E = 5.0 V/m rms, B = 1.7e-8 T rms, energy density 2.2e-10 J/m³. A 0.3 m cube holds about 6e-12 J, replaced every L/c = 1 ns. At the panel's full drive (+8.1 dBm) the figures are 0.0057 W/m² and 1.5 V/m.
findings.source: derivation: S = EIRP/(4πr²), E = sqrt(Z0·S), u = S/c; /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ascalva--claude-spares-spare-iFcbz1/8b6bf486-3081-448c-8f46-b00ba3ebceb0/scratchpad/field_uses/results.json; EIRP values from REDESIGN.md section 7

findings.topic: Stability: the self-sustaining case is plasma
findings.claim: In a slightly resistive plasma, magnetic helicity is nearly conserved while energy decays, giving the force-free Taylor state (curl B = λB). Spheromaks and reversed-field pinches operate in or near it, and Madison Symmetric Torus measurements support helicity conservation. This needs currents in a conducting medium, so it has no free-space radio counterpart.
findings.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_state ; https://cptc.wisc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/327/2017/09/UW-CPTC_15-6.pdf ; original: Taylor, PRL 33, 1139 (1974), https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.33.1139 (DOI from memory)

findings.claim: A doughnut beam with a phase singularity transfers orbital angular momentum to trapped absorbing particles (1-5 µm CuO), which spin; reversing the singularity's sign reverses the spin.
findings.source: https://biomedicaloptics.spiedigitallibrary.org/conference-proceedings-of-spie/2792/0000/Transfer-of-angular-momentum-to-absorbing-particles-from-a-laser/10.1117/12.239174.full ; He et al., PRL 75, 826 (1995), https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.75.826 (DOI from memory)

findings.claim: STED microscopy uses a doughnut-shaped depletion beam so that only the dark centre fluoresces, beating the diffraction limit (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2014). Blue-detuned doughnut beams trap cold atoms in the dark core.
findings.source: https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2014/press-release/ ; Kuga et al., PRL 78, 4713 (1997), https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.4713 (both URLs from memory, not fetched this session)

findings.claim: Framed polarisation knots have been generated and used to encode information via prime factorisation. Microwave toroidal pulses launched from a broadband horn carry skyrmion textures with skyrmion number near ±1 that persist on propagation. For radio, however, orbital-angular-momentum channels are a subset of ordinary MIMO and add no capacity.
findings.source: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-18792-z ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.01765 ; https://lup.lub.lu.se/record/2062936

findings.claim: Radiation force is negligible at this scale. Total force on a perfect absorber is P/c = 1.6e-11 N for 4.7 mW radiated (18.75 dBm EIRP less an assumed 12 dB array gain). Pressure at 0.3 m is 2.2e-10 Pa, about 1e5 below the 20 µPa hearing threshold. Gradient force on a 1 mm water drop in a full-contrast pattern is about 4e-17 N against 4.1e-5 N of weight (ratio 1e-12); for a 50 µm dust grain the ratio is about 3e-13 and the trap depth is 0.02 kT.
findings.source: derivation: F = P/c, p = S/c, U = ½·α·E² with α = 4π·ε0·a³·(εr−1)/(εr+2), F ≈ U/(λ/4); results.json in the scratch folder. Estimate: 12 dB array gain, εr = 77 for water, 5 for dust.

findings.claim: Orbital-angular-momentum torque is τ = l·P/ω: 3.1e-13 N·m per unit l at 2.45 GHz and 1.3e-13 N·m at 5.8 GHz for 4.7 mW; 3.6e-12 N·m at 433 MHz for 9.8 mW. A frictionless 1 g, 5 cm radius foil disc would take about 2 hours for its first turn at 2.45 GHz. The published microwave experiment measured about 1e-8 N·m on a 30 cm copper ring, roughly 3e4 times more; P/ω implies tens of watts for that torque at about 870 MHz (my inference, not the paper's stated power).
findings.source: derivation in results.json; https://www.pubmed.gov/24580592/ ; https://hal-univ-rennes1.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00998554

findings.topic: Why tweezers work in optics and not radio
findings.claim: The force budget P/c is wavelength-independent (10 mW gives 33 pN at any frequency), but an object matched to the wavelength scales in mass as λ³: (12 cm / 1 µm)³ ≈ 1.7e15. A 1 µm bead weighs about 5 fN, so piconewtons dominate; a centimetre object weighs millinewtons. Raising power does not rescue it: the FCC general-population limit of 1.0 mW/cm² at 1.5-100 GHz (f/1500 mW/cm² at 300-1500 MHz) gives only 3.3e-8 Pa.
findings.source: derivation; exposure limit: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-1/subpart-I/section-1.1310

findings.claim: No. A 1 GeV proton has rigidity 5.66 T·m. In 30 µT its gyroradius is about 190 km, small against a magnetosphere tens of thousands of km deep, which is why a weak field shields a planet. A 1 m gyroradius needs about 5.7 T static. The array's field is 1.7e-8 T rms and alternates at GHz, so deflection averages out; electron ponderomotive energy is 3e-9 eV at 3 V/m and 1.4e-6 eV even at 61 V/m.
findings.source: derivation: Bρ = p/q, Up = e²E0²/(4mω²); results.json. Earth surface field 25-65 µT: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth%27s_magnetic_field (from memory, not fetched)

findings.claim: The shift is Δf = l·Ω/2π (total angular momentum, (l+σ)Ω, when polarisation spin is included) and does not depend on the carrier frequency. It was first measured with millimetre waves, shown for spinning objects with light, and reproduced at radio frequency: 24.83 Hz measured at 50π rad/s with l = 1, error 0.67 %.
findings.source: https://physicstoday.aip.org/quick-study/a-new-twist-on-the-doppler-shift ; https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/85025 ; https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.81.4828 ; https://doi.org/10.1364/OL.41.002549 ; https://digital-library.theiet.org/content/journals/10.1049/el.2019.0942

findings.topic: Rotational Doppler: numbers for this array
findings.claim: The same shift applies at 2.4 and 5.8 GHz: 1200 rpm gives 20/40/60/80 Hz for l = 1/2/3/4; 3000 rpm gives 50 Hz per l; 10,000 rpm gives 167 Hz per l. For comparison, linear Doppler is 16.3 Hz per m/s at 2.44 GHz and 38.7 Hz per m/s at 5.8 GHz, and a 15 cm blade tip at 1200 rpm seen edge-on gives ±307 Hz and ±729 Hz. Echo power at 1 m from 0.01 m² with 18.75 dBm EIRP and 12 dBi receive gain is about -40 dBm (2.45 GHz) and -48 dBm (5.8 GHz), so transmit leakage and clutter set the limit, not thermal noise.
findings.source: derivation: Δf = lΩ/2π, 2v/λ, radar equation; results.json. Estimate: 0.01 m² modulated cross-section, 12 dBi receive gain.

findings.topic: Rotational Doppler: how to do it with this hardware
findings.claim: No vortex transmit is needed. Illuminate plainly on the rotation axis, receive on a ring, and take the spatial DFT around the ring; mode l shows a line at l·Ω/2π whose sign gives the rotation sense, which a single on-axis antenna cannot see. The carrier sets the number of resolvable modes, about k·R·sinθ. Estimates for a 15 cm rotor at 0.5 m: 112 mm ring about 2 modes at 2.44 GHz and 4 at 5.8 GHz; 225 mm ring about 3 and 7. Four simultaneous channels resolve l = 0, ±1 (±2 aliased); the 8-whip rings resolve |l| ≤ 3 by time-switching, valid for steady rotation. Transmitting l = 1 from the 4x4 panel's outer ring would put the cone at 53° (2.44 GHz) or 20° (5.8 GHz) off axis.
findings.source: estimate: scattered azimuthal harmonic m ∝ J_m(kR·sinθ); cone angle from first maximum of J_l(ka·sinθ); ring radii and 25 mm pitch from REDESIGN.md section 4; results.json

findings.claim: The radio counterpart of the STED doughnut is the monopulse or null-steering null. Location precision scales as beamwidth/(k·sqrt(2·SNR)): a 25° beam gives about 1.1° at 20 dB SNR and 0.11° at 40 dB. Quiet zones for interference rejection are the same physics. This is the most practically useful structured-field capability of the array.
findings.source: estimate: standard monopulse accuracy formula with slope k ≈ 1.6; background https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopulse_radar (from memory, not fetched)

findings.claim: By physics reality and demo value: (1) rotational Doppler of a fan or drill by receive-mode decomposition; (2) null steering, quiet zones and null-based direction finding; (3) near-field focal-spot power or information targeting within about 1 m; (4) mapping a knotted or vortex null with a moving probe, as a visual demo with no application yet; (5) vortex-mode multiplexing, real but equal to MIMO and decaying fast off axis; (6) torque, real but about 3e-13 N·m; (7) trapping or shielding, effectively zero. Polarisation-structure material probing is blocked because the panel is single-polarisation and the whips are vertical.
findings.source: synthesis of the findings above; polarisation constraint from REDESIGN.md section 4

open_questions: Neither local_fields.md nor fields_study.md existed when I looked, so overlap with the parallel studies (especially the optimiser's knotted-vortex attempt and the vortex-beam section) is unchecked.
Radiated power was taken as EIRP minus an assumed 12 dB array gain (6 dB for four whips); force and torque figures scale directly with the real value.

Rotational Doppler mode counts are a J_m(kR sin θ) estimate, not a simulation. A short simulation of a rotating scatterer seen by the 8-whip and 4-channel rings would confirm line amplitudes and off-axis mode crosstalk.

Can the time-switched 8- or 16-whip ring (four slots) hold coherence well enough across slots for mode decomposition at 20-200 Hz offsets, and how much does transmit leakage and phase noise within 200 Hz of the carrier limit the measurement?
The whips are specified for 0.4-2.3 GHz and described as usable to 6 GHz; their pattern and matching at 2.44 and 5.8 GHz for a ring receive experiment are unverified.

Several citations are DOIs or URLs from memory, not fetched this session: Taylor 1974, He 1995, Kuga 1997, the Nobel 2014 page, and the Wikipedia pages for Earth's field and monopulse radar. The transmit power used in the Emile torque experiment was not confirmed.
